entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280 BCE, Soli – c. 207 BCE, Athens) stands as the pivotal third head of the Stoic school, often credited with systematizing and defending its doctrines so comprehensively that he effectively served as its second founder. Operating within the vibrant intellectual landscape of Hellenistic Athens, Chrysippus transformed Stoicism from a nascent philosophy into a formidable intellectual system, influencing generations of thinkers across the Mediterranean world. His prolific output and rigorous logical arguments provided the bedrock for Stoic thought in ethics, physics, and epistemology, ensuring its prominence amidst rival schools like the Epicureans and Skeptics.

Born in Soli, Cilicia, Chrysippus journeyed to Athens where he became a student of Cleanthes, the successor to Zeno of Citium. He authored an astonishing estimated 700 works, primarily in logic, physics, and ethics, though tragically, only fragments survive today, preserved mainly through later doxographers such as Diogenes Laërtius and Plutarch. Chrysippus significantly advanced propositional logic, developing a sophisticated system that explored truth functions and inference rules, which remarkably prefigured elements of modern logic. He also offered robust defenses of Stoic determinism and a pantheistic cosmology, integrating these with a compelling ethical framework centered on living in accordance with universal reason and virtue.
